Here are the verse-by-verse notes compiled from the sources retrieved:

## Genesis 41:29–57 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 29 — Seven Years of Great Abundance

- **Traditional Reading:** Joseph interprets the seven good cows and seven good ears as seven years of extraordinary plenty throughout all Egypt. Gill notes this meant "not only a sufficiency but an abundance, even to luxury," observing that such plenty occurred when the Nile rose to sixteen cubits, and that God alone could cause seven such years in succession. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/41.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The years would be so plentiful that they would be "great" — not just enough, but abundant. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)
- **Reformed (Piper/Desiring God):** Piper emphasizes that the writer makes it clear, by repeating it three times (vv. 25, 28, 32), that both the prosperity *and* the famine are "the work of God, not mere nature." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/does-god-intend-evil-for-our-good)

### v. 30 — The Famine Will Follow and Consume

- **Traditional Reading:** The seven years of famine that follow will be so severe that "all the plenty shall be forgotten." The Pulpit Commentary renders the Hebrew literally: "the famine should consume, or make an end of, the land." The famine would erase all memory of the good years. (StudyLight.org, Pulpit Commentary excerpt)
- **Gill:** The famine was likely caused by the Nile failing to overflow; when it rose less than twelve cubits, famine ensued. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/41.htm)

### v. 31 — The Severity of the Famine

- **Traditional Reading:** The Hebrew phrasing is emphatic — literally "the plenty will not be known in the land from the face of that famine, for it will be very grievous." The Pulpit Commentary notes "from the face of" is used of the efficient cause: the famine itself will be the reason the plenty is forgotten. (StudyLight.org, Pulpit Commentary excerpt)

### v. 32 — The Dream Repeated Twice: Certainty and Imminence

- **Traditional Reading:** Joseph explains that the doubling of Pharaoh's dream confirms that "the thing is established by God" — literally "the word is firmly fixed, i.e., certainly decreed by the Elohim." The Pulpit Commentary adds: "and hastening is the Elohim to do it." (StudyLight.org, Pulpit Commentary excerpt)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Joseph saw God's confirmation in the repetition — the principle later codified in Deuteronomy 19:15 ("by the mouth of two or three witnesses the matter shall be established"). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)
- **Bible.org:** Both dreams were given to indicate the certainty of what was to occur. The "seven" in each dream was the time involved — seven years. (https://bible.org/seriespage/pit-palace-genesis-411-57)

### v. 33 — Joseph Advises Pharaoh to Choose a Discerning Man

- **Traditional Reading:** Joseph transitions from prophet to counselor. The Hebrew for "discerning" (נָבוֹן, *navon*) means intelligent, perceptive — able to understand and act. "Wise" (חָכָם) adds the practical skill to implement. (Pulpit Commentary via StudyLight.org)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Guzik draws the distinction between knowledge and wisdom: "Knowledge tells what is going on; wisdom tells what to do about it. Knowledge is the diagnosis; wisdom is directed to the cure." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)
- **Bible.org:** Joseph was "more than a prophet; he was an administrator." He not only foretold what was coming but "was also competent to analyze the situation and determine the best course of action." The author adds: "it never entered into his mind that he should be the one appointed over this project." (https://bible.org/seriespage/pit-palace-genesis-411-57)

### v. 34 — Appoint Commissioners and Take a Fifth

- **Traditional Reading:** "Let him fifth the land" — i.e., levy a 20% tax on produce during the seven plentiful years. The Pulpit Commentary notes this was double the normal annual impost (normally 10%), but the unprecedented fertility made it bearable. Diodorus Siculus mentions the payment of a fifth in productive years as a primitive custom. (StudyLight.org, Pulpit Commentary excerpt)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Guzik notes the plan required proper administration: the problem understood, the goal formulated, the right people appointed, everyone understanding their role, oversight, and measurement. "God would use a man to put all that into place — it wouldn't happen by what we normally think of as a miracle." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)
- **B.W. Johnson:** A 20% tax would not be excessive "in a country where seventy per cent has often been taken with no excuse." (StudyLight.org, B.W. Johnson excerpt)

### v. 35 — Collecting Under Pharaoh's Authority

- **Traditional Reading:** The food was to be gathered "under the hand of Pharaoh" — i.e., under royal authority — and stored in the cities. The Pulpit Commentary renders this: "let them keep food in the cities, and let them keep it." The grain would be public property administered by the crown, not private hoarding. (StudyLight.org, Pulpit Commentary excerpt)

### v. 36 — The Reserve to Prevent Perishing

- **Traditional Reading:** "That the land perish not" — literally, "and the land (i.e., the people of the land) shall not be cut off in, or by, the famine." The plan was to prevent national extinction. (StudyLight.org, Pulpit Commentary)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "The message of God through Pharaoh's dreams was of a true crisis to come. If they did not prepare, the land would perish." Guzik adds the quote from Barnhouse: "God always works through men performing tasks on the earth." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)

### v. 37 — The Proposal Pleased Pharaoh and His Officials

- **Traditional Reading:** The advice found immediate and unanimous approval. Ellicott notes that Pharaoh and his servants recognized not only the truth of Joseph's words but also that Joseph was the instrument through whom God had spoken. (BibleHub, Ellicott excerpt from search results)

### v. 38 — "A Man in Whom the Spirit of God Abides"

- **Traditional Reading:** This is the first mention in Scripture of the Holy Spirit coming upon a person. Pharaoh, a pagan, recognized something divine in Joseph. Ellicott comments: "Pharaoh now recognises the truth of Joseph's words, but sees also in him the instrument by which Elohim had spoken." (BibleHub, Ellicott excerpt)
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** "The truth of Joseph's words is so evident that the king of Egypt recognizes the Holy Spirit's presence with him. Of course, pagan notions probably color the pharaoh's conception... He is speaking with more wisdom than he knows, just like Caiaphas did when he spoke of Jesus' death as a substitution (John 11:45–53)." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josephs-ascendancy)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Pharaoh had access to plenty of priests, magicians, and holy men. What he did not have (until Joseph) was a man with the Spirit of God." Pharaoh recognized this "not through a sermon or showy miracle, but through practical discernment — character, humility, knowledge, and wisdom." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)
- **B.W. Johnson:** Notes there are "indications in the monumental history of Egypt that before and beyond the Egyptian idolatry there was a belief in the one great God," so Pharaoh's partial acknowledgment of Joseph's God is not surprising. (StudyLight.org, B.W. Johnson excerpt)

### v. 39 — None as Discerning and Wise as Joseph

- **Traditional Reading:** Pharaoh's conclusion is rational: if God has shown Joseph all this, then the Spirit of God must be in him, making him uniquely discerning and wise. B.W. Johnson notes: "His words show how greatly the Egyptians esteemed the higher knowledge, since it confirms the opinion that made this nation so renowned among the ancients. The 'wisdom of Egypt' was everywhere celebrated." (StudyLight.org, B.W. Johnson excerpt)

### v. 40 — Joseph Over Pharaoh's House, Second Only to the Throne

- **Traditional Reading:** "All my people shall be ruled according to your word" — the Hebrew verb here (יִשַּׁק, *yishaq*) usually means "to kiss," but here has the special sense of "dispose or order their conduct." Ellicott explains that "only in the throne will I be greater than you" means "in all that concerns my royal rank, dignity, and rights." (BibleHub, Ellicott excerpt)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Joseph was over Pharaoh's personal business (his house), would rule all the people of Egypt, and would be second in the kingdom. Guzik notes that Joseph's journey "from the pit to the pinnacle took 13 hard years." Promotion is from the Lord (Psalm 75:6–7). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)

### v. 41 — "I Hereby Place You Over All the Land of Egypt"

- **Traditional Reading:** This formal declaration confirms the investiture. Gill notes that Joseph was "appointed chief over the kingdom next to Pharaoh." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/41.htm)
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** "After years of faithfulness in little things — obeying Jacob, serving Potiphar, and managing the prison — Joseph is finally given authority over much (Matt. 25:14–30)." John Chrysostom is quoted: "Joseph bore distress with endurance; endurance gave him character; having such character he acted in hope, and hope did not disappoint him." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josephs-ascendancy)

### v. 42 — Signet Ring, Fine Linen, Gold Chain

- **Traditional Reading:** The signet ring conveyed delegated royal authority — Joseph could now issue decrees in Pharaoh's name. The "vestures of fine linen" reflected Egyptian culture: "Egypt was celebrated for its flax, and for the fineness of its textures. The priests were arrayed in official robes of linen, and no man was allowed to enter a temple in a woolen garment" (Herodotus ii.37, cited in Barnes/StudyLight.org excerpt).
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Guzik draws a strong contrast: "Once he wore the shackles of a prisoner; now he had the signet ring of Pharaoh. Once Joseph had the rags of a dungeon; now he had wonderful apparel... Once Joseph walked as a slave; now he traveled in style." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)

### v. 43 — The Second Chariot and "Bow the Knee!"

- **Traditional Reading:** Joseph rode in the "second chariot" — Pharaoh's own secondary chariot, a public display of his rank. The cry before him (אַבְרֵךְ, *avrech*) is translated "Bow the knee!" though its exact meaning is debated. The Pulpit Commentary and others see it as a proclamation of homage. (StudyLight.org)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Joseph "once could only obey orders; now he could also give orders." Guzik sees in Joseph a picture of Christ: "In Jesus believers are given authority, apparel, adornment, and affluence." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)

### v. 44 — "Without Your Permission, No One Shall Lift Hand or Foot"

- **Traditional Reading:** A Hebraism expressing absolute authority under Pharaoh alone. The phrase "lift his hand or foot" means to undertake any action whatsoever. Ellicott and others see this as the formal delegation of executive power. (StudyLight.org)

### v. 45 — Zaphenath-paneah and Asenath

- **Traditional Reading on the Name:** The meaning of Zaphenath-paneah is uncertain. Older Jewish legends (noted by Guzik) said each letter represented a quality: "Seer – redeemer – prophet – supporter – interpreter of dreams – clever – discreet – wise." More likely, it means "God speaks and He lives" (so Steindorff, cited by Bible.org and Ligonier).
- **Traditional Reading on Asenath:** She was the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On (Heliopolis), the center of sun-god Ra worship. The name Potiphera is distinct from Potiphar (Joseph's former master); Bible.org says there is "absolutely no reason to see any connection... other than a similarity of sound." (https://bible.org/seriespage/pit-palace-genesis-411-57)
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** The marriage "further established" Joseph's position, linking him to the priestly elite of Egypt. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josephs-ascendancy)
- **Bible.org (Evangelical):** Addresses the concern about Joseph marrying an Egyptian: "Had you been Joseph, where would you have gone to find a godly wife? Would you have gone to Judah, who was willing to sleep with a Canaanite cult prostitute?... God had not yet given any commandments regarding marriage... Only marriage to a Canaanite woman was later forbidden." (https://bible.org/seriespage/pit-palace-genesis-411-57)
- **Jewish legend (noted by Guzik):** Some fabrications claim Asenath was really the daughter of Dinah and Shechem, abandoned at Egypt's border and adopted by the priest. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)

### v. 46 — Joseph Was Thirty Years Old

- **Traditional Reading:** Joseph was sold into slavery at 17 (Gen 37:2), spent 13 years as slave and prisoner, and now at 30 entered Pharaoh's service. Gill notes the chronology: he was about 28 when interpreting the butler's and baker's dreams two years earlier. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/41.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Joseph was a young man to have such authority. Yet he had been in God's school of trust-deepening and character-development for a long time." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)
- **Bible.org:** "Joseph did nothing different in Pharaoh's palace than he did in Potiphar's penthouse or in his prison. In every instance Joseph exercised his God-given ability to administrate." (https://bible.org/seriespage/pit-palace-genesis-411-57)

### v. 47 — The Land Brought Forth Bountifully

- **Traditional Reading:** The fulfillment is recorded succinctly. The Pulpit Commentary notes this confirms Joseph's prophetic character: "the fulfillment is as perfect in the one part [abundance] as in the other [famine]." (StudyLight.org, Pulpit Commentary excerpt)

### vv. 48–49 — Storing Grain Beyond Measure

- **Traditional Reading:** Joseph collected "all the excess food" — likely both the 20% tax *and* purchased grain (Ellicott: "besides the fifth paid as tax... Joseph bought corn largely during these years when it was at its cheapest"). The hyperbole "like the sand of the sea" and "beyond measure" stresses the staggering quantity. (BibleHub, Ellicott excerpt)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** This "was a significant logistic and accounting challenge: to gather, measure, account for, and store very much grain." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)

### v. 50 — Two Sons Born Before the Famine

- **Traditional Reading:** The sons were born during the seven years of plenty — Manasseh first, then Ephraim. The Pulpit Commentary suggests the birth of Ephraim was likely near the end of the seven years. (StudyLight.org)

### v. 51 — Manasseh: "God Made Me Forget"

- **Traditional Reading:** The name Manasseh (מְנַשֶּׁה) means "causing to forget." Gill and others see this as Joseph's gratitude to God for enabling him to forget his past toil and suffering. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/41.htm)
- **Bible.org:** "I do not think that this should be understood in a negative way as though Joseph had no more interest or concern for [his family]. Certainly God's rich blessings had enabled him to blot out the painful memories of the past, especially the hurt and bitterness which could only harbor a grudge against his brothers." The paraphrase offered: "God has made me forget all my trouble *with* my father's household." The bitterness was gone, enabling Joseph later to deal with his brothers without vengeance. (https://bible.org/seriespage/pit-palace-genesis-411-57)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "God's people can't be doubly fruitful until they are also forgetting." Guzik quotes C.S. Lewis's *The Great Divorce*: hell is a place where no one forgets anything — "remembering every slight, every cruel exchange of words." In heaven, "all these things are put away because all things have become new." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)

### v. 52 — Ephraim: "God Made Me Fruitful in Affliction"

- **Traditional Reading:** Ephraim (אֶפְרַיִם) means "double fruit." Joseph acknowledges that God caused him to prosper in the very land where he had suffered. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/41.htm)
- **Bible.org:** "To Joseph, affliction and blessing were not contradictory, for God was able to turn sorrow into joy." (https://bible.org/seriespage/pit-palace-genesis-411-57)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The sequence is important — forgetfulness (Manasseh) before fruitfulness (Ephraim): one must learn to release past pain before one can be truly fruitful. Both sons received Hebrew names, not Egyptian — Joseph "did not forget the faith of his fathers." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)

### v. 53 — The Seven Years of Plenty Ended

- **Traditional Reading:** The Pulpit Commentary simply notes: "the seven years of plenteousness, that was in the land of Egypt, were ended." The transition was exact, as Joseph had predicted. (StudyLight.org, Pulpit Commentary excerpt)

### v. 54 — The Famine Began "Just as Joseph Had Said"

- **Traditional Reading:** The famine was not limited to Egypt: "the dearth was in all lands" — i.e., adjoining countries: Syria, Arabia, Palestine, Canaan. Egypt alone had bread because of Joseph's preparation. Ellicott notes that since the Nile at this period was not regulated by dams and canals, famines were more common. The Pulpit Commentary adds a historical parallel: a terrible famine in AD 1064–1071 under the Fatimee Khaleefeh El-Mustansir, when "people ate corpses and animals that died of themselves." (StudyLight.org, Pulpit Commentary excerpt)

### v. 55 — "Go to Joseph and Do Whatever He Tells You"

- **Traditional Reading:** When the Egyptians cried to Pharaoh, he directed them to Joseph — a striking acknowledgment of Joseph's authority. The Pulpit Commentary cross-references the famine in Samaria (2 Kings 6:26) as a similar public desperation. (StudyLight.org, Pulpit Commentary excerpt)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Pharaoh has had reason to trust Joseph more and more, and now he adheres to his purpose of sending his people to him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)

### v. 56 — Joseph Opened the Storehouses and Sold Grain

- **Traditional Reading:** The stores "under Pharaoh's hand were public property, obtained either by lawful taxation or by purchase." Joseph sold — he did not give away — the grain. The Barnes/StudyLight.org notes emphasize: "It was a great public benefit to sell this grain, that had been providently kept in store, at a moderate price, and thus preserve the lives of a nation." (StudyLight.org)
- **Reformed (Piper/Desiring God):** Piper sees God's sovereignty throughout: "God is bringing this famine, which will threaten the existence of his chosen people. All the while laying a 22-year plan for rescuing his people from his own threatened destruction." Joseph had now been in Egypt 13 years, and the seven years of plenty had passed; two more years into the famine, the brothers would arrive (Gen 45:6) — 22 years total. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/does-god-intend-evil-for-our-good)

### v. 57 — All Nations Came to Joseph

- **Traditional Reading:** "All countries" means the neighboring nations — Syria, Arabia, Palestine, Canaan, etc. "All the earth" is a relative expression meaning the known world of that region. Gill adds: "It is thought by many, that for this care of Joseph in laying up provision... he was worshipped by them under various names; as the Apis, which was an ox, a sign of fruitfulness; and Serapis, sometimes figured as a young man carrying a basket of bread on his head." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/41.htm)
- **Gill (Christological Typology):** "He was an eminent type of Christ in all this... as Joseph was raised to great honour and glory in Pharaoh's court, so Christ was exalted by his Father... if the new name given him, 'Zaphnathpaaneah', signifies the Saviour of the world... it agrees well with Christ... and as Joseph had all the stores of corn under his care, and the needy were bid to go to him for it, so Christ has all the treasures of grace in his hand." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/41.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "The people in Canaan — including Joseph's family — also suffered from the famine. But God made wise (though unexpected) provision for them by sending Joseph ahead of the family." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/)

## Summary of Distinctive Protestant Traditions

| Topic | Distinctive Reading |
|---|---|
| **God's Sovereignty over the Famine (Reformed – Piper, Ligonier)** | Piper stresses that God *himself* brought the famine as part of His sovereign plan, not merely permitted it: "God is bringing this famine, which will threaten the existence of his chosen people... He brings his own people into the life-threatening danger of extinction, all the while planning their unimaginable rescue." Ligonier frames Joseph as a type of Christ, empowered by the Spirit to rule — the same Spirit given to Christ and now to believers. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/does-god-intend-evil-for-our-good; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josephs-ascendancy) |
| **Faithfulness in Secular Work (Evangelical – Bible.org)** | Emphasizes that God saved His people not through a priest or prophet but through an *administrator*. "Let us beware of categorizing occupations in such a way as to make some more spiritual than others. Everyone is a full-time minister in the Scriptures." Joseph was promoted for his skill, not just his spirituality. (https://bible.org/seriespage/pit-palace-genesis-411-57) |
| **The Spirit of God in Joseph (Pentecostal/Charismatic – Enduring Word/Guzik)** | Guzik highlights this as "the first mention in the Bible of the Holy Spirit coming upon a man," with emphasis on the Spirit's practical manifestation — "not through a sermon or showy miracle, but through practical discernment." The Spirit's presence was visible in character, wisdom, and humility. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/) |
| **Joseph as Type of Christ (Baptist – Gill)** | Gill draws an extended typological parallel: Joseph falsely accused like Christ, imprisoned like Christ, exalted like Christ; his new name meaning "saviour of the world"; the hungry sent to him for bread just as the needy come to Christ for grace. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/41.htm) |
| **Forgetting Before Fruitfulness (Pastoral – Guzik)** | Manasseh (forgetting) before Ephraim (fruitfulness): "God's people can't be doubly fruitful until they are also forgetting." This is a distinctive pastoral application from the charismatic/Pentecostal tradition. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/) |
